title: Sample size expansion as the mechanism to reduce Type II error and boost test power
scenario_markdown:
An aerospace materials lab conducts quality acceptance testing on titanium alloy turbine fasteners. The specification requires tensile strength of at least $500\text{ MPa}$ ($H_0: \mu \ge 500\text{ MPa}$ vs. $H_1: \mu < 500\text{ MPa}$). With significance level set at $\alpha = 0.05$ and an initial sample size of $n = 25$ fasteners, the probability of a Type II error for detecting a true mean of $490\text{ MPa}$ is $\beta = 0.28$ (statistical power $1 - \beta = 0.72$).

The chief safety engineer requires reducing the risk of releasing non-conforming fasteners ($\\beta$) to no more than $0.05$ ($5\%$), while maintaining the false alarm rate at $\alpha = 0.05$. Analyze how changing the sample size $n$ affects $\beta$ and statistical power.

parameters.objective: Explain how increasing sample size reduces Type II error probability beta and increases test power while holding alpha constant

assumptions: Significance level alpha is held constant at 0.05
Tensile strength distribution has known or stable standard deviation sigma
Standard error of the mean is SE = sigma / sqrt(n)

approval.notes: Reviewed conceptual alignment: At fixed alpha = 0.05, increasing n from 25 to 100 shrinks SE by half, separating the null and alternative sampling distributions. This drives beta down from 0.28 to < 0.05 and boosts power (1 - beta) from 0.72 to > 0.95. Proves that increasing sample size is the only way to reduce beta without inflating alpha.

stages.prompt_markdown: If the laboratory quadruples its sample size from $n = 25$ to $n = 100$ while maintaining $\alpha = 0.05$, what happens to the Type II error probability $\beta$ and test power $1 - \beta$?

options.text_markdown: **$\beta$ decreases significantly and test power $1 - \beta$ increases**: The test becomes far more capable of detecting sub-standard alloy batches.
**$\beta$ increases and power decreases**: More data creates more opportunities for sampling errors.
options.hint_markdown: Larger samples reduce standard error, making tests more accurate and powerful, not more error-prone.

options.text_markdown: **$\beta$ is completely unaffected**: $\beta$ is determined solely by the chosen $\alpha$ level and does not depend on sample size.
options.hint_markdown: Sample size directly determines the overlap between the null and alternative distributions, directly controlling $\beta$.

stages.explanation_markdown: Increasing sample size $n$ narrows the standard error of the mean ($SE = \sigma / \sqrt{n}$). With a smaller standard error, both the null and alternative sampling distributions become much tighter with far less mutual overlap. At a fixed significance level $\alpha = 0.05$, this reduction in overlap drastically shrinks $\beta$ (Type II error) and increases statistical power ($1 - \beta$).

stages.prompt_markdown: What mathematical mechanism explains why increasing $n$ reduces $\beta$ at fixed $\alpha$?

options.text_markdown: **Standard error shrinks ($SE = \sigma/\sqrt{n}$)**: As $n$ grows, the spread of sample means under both $H_0$ and $H_1$ narrows, moving the non-rejection region farther away from the true mean under $H_1$.
**The critical value moves to infinity**: Larger $n$ shifts the critical value so far out that rejection becomes impossible.
options.hint_markdown: At $\alpha = 0.05$, the critical $Z$ value remains fixed at $-1.645$ (or approaches it for $t$ tests); it does not diverge.

options.text_markdown: **The true population variance $\sigma^2$ is compressed to zero**: Surveying more items alters the physical properties of the titanium alloy.
options.hint_markdown: Population parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are fixed physical constants; only the standard error of the sample mean shrinks.

stages.explanation_markdown: Under the Central Limit Theorem, the spread of the sample mean is $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$. Quadrupling $n$ from $25$ to $100$ cuts the standard error in half. Consequently, the distribution of $\bar{x}$ when $\mu = 490$ has very little probability area extending into the non-rejection region of the null hypothesis ($\\bar{x} \ge 500 - 1.645 \sigma_{\\bar{x}}$), driving $\beta$ toward zero.

stages.prompt_markdown: For a fixed sample size $n$, decreasing $\alpha$ always increases $\beta$. Why is increasing sample size $n$ unique in statistical decision theory?

options.text_markdown: **It is the only operational method to reduce both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ simultaneously**: Increasing data collection provides more statistical information, allowing the decision maker to shrink Type I error and Type II error at the same time.
**It eliminates all statistical error entirely**: Any sample with $n \ge 100$ guarantees $\alpha = 0$ and $\beta = 0$.
options.hint_markdown: As long as sampling is used rather than a census, random sampling variation remains, so error probabilities never reach absolute zero.

options.text_markdown: **It automatically proves the null hypothesis is true**: Large samples confirm $H_0$ as absolute truth.
options.hint_markdown: Sample size does not alter truth; it simply gives the test greater acuity to detect departures from the null.

stages.explanation_markdown: With a fixed sample size, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are locked in an inescapable inverse trade-off: lowering the false alarm rate ($\alpha$) inevitably increases missed detections ($\beta$). **Increasing sample size $n$ is the only tool that breaks this trade-off**, because adding genuine empirical information reduces total sampling uncertainty, allowing researchers to achieve both a low $\alpha$ (e.g. $0.01$) and high power (e.g. $1 - \beta = 0.99$) simultaneously.
